source: Evans, Barston & Pollard (1983) On the conflict between logic and belief in syllogistic reasoning
finding: Belief bias paradigm: people accept conclusions they find believable even when logically invalid. Logic and belief conflict.
numbers: Acceptance rates (approx, from memory): valid-believable 89%, invalid-believable 71%, valid-unbelievable 56%, invalid-unbelievable 10%. Logic effect larger for unbelievable conclusions (interaction).
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session. Exact N not verified. Later work (Dube, Rotello & Heit 2010) argues the interaction is a response-bias artefact.
agent_relevance: Fluent belief-consistent answers pass unchecked. Agent needs a check that does not lean on its own prior belief.

source: Wason & Evans (1975) Dual processes in reasoning?
finding: Origin of the dual-process idea in reasoning: on the selection task, stated reasons rationalise choices made on other grounds (matching bias).
numbers: Most people pick matching cards (P and Q); stated reasons did not predict choice. Small samples (from memory).
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session. Tiny samples. The rationalisation reading was later contested.
agent_relevance: Model self-explanations may be post hoc rationalisation of an answer already chosen. Explanation is not proof the answer was derived.

source: Sloman (1996) The empirical case for two systems of reasoning
finding: Proposes an associative system and a rule-based system. Key evidence: simultaneous contradictory belief (Criterion S), e.g. Linda, where the representativeness pull persists while the person knows the conjunction rule.
numbers: No single number; review of many studies.
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session. Criterion S is weak evidence for two systems; one system with conflicting cues could do the same.
agent_relevance: Agent can hold two candidate answers (fast and checked) and must reconcile them explicitly; agreement test between attempts.

source: Epstein (1994) Integration of the cognitive and psychodynamic unconscious (CEST)
finding: Cognitive-experiential self-theory: an experiential system (fast, affective, associative) and a rational system. Source of the Rational-Experiential Inventory.
numbers: No effect sizes recalled with confidence.
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session. REI scales correlate only weakly with CRT in later work.
agent_relevance: Another statement that intuition and analysis are separable but interacting.

source: Evans & Over (1996) Rationality and Reasoning
finding: Implicit tacit processes versus explicit analytic ones; rationality1 (reaching goals) versus rationality2 (following rules). Heuristic-analytic framework is default-interventionist: heuristics pick relevant content, the analytic stage may or may not intervene.
numbers: Book; no single experiment.
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Success should be judged by goal outcome, not by rule following.

source: Stanovich & West (2000) Individual differences in reasoning: implications for the rationality debate
finding: Coined the labels System 1 and System 2. Across many heuristics-and-biases tasks, cognitive ability correlates positively with normative answers, and thinking dispositions add independent variance.
numbers: Correlations of ability with normative performance typically about r=.25 to .40 (from memory); some tasks show none or reversed.
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session. Varies by task; the 'smart people are less biased' pattern has exceptions (bias blind spot).
agent_relevance: Bigger models are more normative on some tasks; capability alone is no guarantee. Check on the specific task class.

source: Kahneman & Frederick (2002) Representativeness revisited: attribute substitution in intuitive judgment
finding: Core mechanism: when the target attribute is hard, System 1 substitutes an easier related attribute; System 2 monitors lazily and often endorses the output. Explains Linda, base-rate neglect, bat and ball.
numbers: Linda conjunction error about 85% in the Tversky and Kahneman 1983 direct test (from memory).
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session. Substitution is a description, not a measured process; hard to falsify (Gigerenzer critique).
agent_relevance: Operational idea for S1: restate the question and ask whether the draft answer answers it, not an easier neighbour.

source: Frederick (2005) Cognitive reflection and decision making
finding: Three-item Cognitive Reflection Test (bat and ball, 5 machines, lily pads). Each has a fast wrong answer (10 cents, 100 minutes, 24 days). Low scorers were more impatient and risk-prone on some tasks.
numbers: Total N=3,428 across sites; 41% correct in the original, verified second-hand via the Hagendorff et al. paper. Per-site means (from memory): MIT about 2.18 of 3, Toledo about 0.57.
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session. Paywalled (403); only N and 41% verified second-hand. Later work shows the CRT also measures numeracy (Sinayev and Peters).
agent_relevance: The CRT is the standard probe for intuition versus reflection. Frontier LLMs now saturate it, so use altered variants.

source: Kahneman (2011) Thinking, Fast and Slow
finding: Popular synthesis. System 1 fast and automatic; System 2 slow, effortful and lazy and mostly endorses System 1 output. Several cited priming and ego-depletion results have since failed to replicate.
numbers: Ego-depletion multi-lab replication (Hagger et al. 2016, 23 labs, N about 2,100): effect d about 0.04, near zero (from memory).
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session. Kahneman himself calls the two systems 'fictions' of convenience.
agent_relevance: Do not import the two-system picture as mechanism. Take operational findings only.

source: Evans & Stanovich (2013) Dual-process theories of higher cognition: advancing the debate
finding: Replies to critics. Type 1 is autonomous and needs no working memory; Type 2 needs working memory and supports hypothetical thinking. Speed, bias and consciousness are correlates, not defining features. Rejects 'Type 1 = biased, Type 2 = correct'.
numbers: Five named misconceptions (from memory). Architectures: default-interventionist versus parallel-competitive.
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session. Critics: Melnikoff & Bargh (2018) say the dichotomy is not coherent; Keren & Schul (2009) say it is unfalsifiable.
agent_relevance: Chain of thought is not correctness. Choose mode by the task-class record, not by dogma.

source: Thompson, Prowse Turner & Pennycook (2011) Intuition, reason and metacognition
finding: Two-response paradigm with feeling-of-rightness (FOR) ratings. Low FOR on the fast answer predicts more rethinking and more answer change.
numbers: Effect sizes not recalled with confidence.
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session. FOR is a rating and may track fluency, not correctness.
agent_relevance: Trigger for G1: rethink on a low confidence or consistency signal.

source: Pennycook, Fugelsang & Koehler (2015) What makes us think? A three-stage dual-process model
finding: Adds a stage between intuitions: conflict detection decides whether to rethink; then either rationalise the first answer or decouple and replace it. Rationalisation is common.
numbers: Model paper; built on earlier timing and confidence data.
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session. Detection and rationalisation are hard to separate behaviourally.
agent_relevance: Template for S4 test and impasse detector. Warning: self-checks often just rationalise.

source: Bago & De Neys (2017) Fast logic? Examining the time course assumption of dual process theory
finding: Two-response, speeded and loaded first answer, then free second answer. Most who ended correct on base-rate and syllogism items had already answered correctly at first. Challenges the claim that logic needs slow System 2.
numbers: About 90% of final correct answers were already correct at the intuitive stage (from memory; several studies).
limits: From memory of the literature; page not opened this session. Exact figures not verified. Items with simple logic only.
agent_relevance: Some right answers are cheap. Draft directly, escalate only if the check fails (G1).

source: De Neys, Cromheeke & Osman (2011) Biased but in doubt: conflict and decision confidence
finding: Even when reasoners gave the biased intuitive answer on base-rate and conjunction problems, their confidence dropped versus no-conflict controls. So bias is not just failure to notice conflict.
numbers: Exp 1 base-rate, N=247 Leuven undergraduates: conflict items correct about 20%, no-conflict about 95%, confidence about 10 points lower on conflict items (F(1,246)=54); same drop for incorrectly solved items. Exp 2 conjunction, N=147: correct about 24% vs about 96% control, again about 10-point drop. Exp 3 younger ages: drop absent in the youngest; oldest group still under 20% accurate.
limits: Confidence is a rating, not a process. Student samples.
agent_relevance: The model may 'know' it is on shaky ground. A calibrated confidence or agreement signal can trigger S4/S5 even when the answer is wrong.

source: Sinayev & Peters (2015) Cognitive reflection vs. calculation in decision making
finding: Split CRT scores into cognitive reflection (override wrong intuition) and calculation (numeric ability). Calculation and numeracy, not reflection, predicted decision-task performance.
numbers: Study 1: N=1,413 US adults (Understanding America Study, 2014). Reflection added no unique explanatory power for framing and conjunction measures; Calculation and numeracy did. Study 2 replicated; no decision bias predicted independently by reflection. CRT measures Calculation more than Reflection.
limits: Online adult samples, correlational; the authors admit low reliability of the reflection score.
agent_relevance: Challenges the view that CRT measures a general override disposition. Part of 'CoT helps' is just computation.

source: Alos-Ferrer, Garagnani & Huegelschaefer (2016) Cognitive reflection, decision biases, and response times
finding: Built conflict, alignment, neutral and heuristic versions of CRT and bias items and timed them. CRT items behave as dual-process theory predicts; classic bias items (base-rate, conjunction, ratio bias) show mixed timing evidence.
numbers: N=158 (101 female, age 18-44, mean about 23). CRT: alignment and heuristic variants faster, neutral slower than conflict originals. Base-rate items had medians above 30 seconds, far slower than CRT.
limits: One lab, incentivised, students. Response time is a weak proxy for process type.
agent_relevance: Slow does not equal System 2. Do not use token count or latency as the signal of deliberation.

source: Croskerry (2013) Cognitive debiasing 1: origins of bias and theory of debiasing
finding: Applied dual-process model of diagnosis: most clinical errors start in Type 1 processing, so debiasing means detecting Type 1 outputs and submitting them to Type 2 verification. Uses Stanovich's grouping of autonomous Type 1 origins.
numbers: Review; no new numbers.
limits: Conceptual; 'slow down' debiasing is weak in trials (see debiasing subfield).
agent_relevance: Medical expert use of the same idea; supports checks on the first answer, not blanket slowing.

source: Djulbegovic, Hozo, Beckstead, Tsalatsanis & Pauker (2012) Dual processing model of medical decision-making
finding: Threshold model: decide by fast Type 1 when confident, escalate to Type 2 otherwise. Notes there are many dual-process theories, in two groups: parallel-competitive and default-interventionist.
numbers: Formal model; no empirical N in the parts read.
limits: Thresholds not empirically calibrated; labels are shorthand, not brain systems.
agent_relevance: Formal template for 'switch when a threshold is crossed'.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models (Studies 1 and 4)
finding: GPT-3 family models show human-like intuitive errors on the CRT and semantic illusions; the more capable ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 stopped making them (hyperrational).
numbers: CRT: original human study n=3,428 41% correct; davinci-003 5% correct and 80% intuitive; ChatGPT-3.5 59% correct, 15% intuitive; ChatGPT-4 96% correct (95% in the published version), 0% intuitive. Humans 55% intuitive on CRT, 64% on illusions. Semantic illusions: davinci-003 fell for it 72%; ChatGPT-4 88% correct.
limits: Items may be in training data; wording changes shift results; OpenAI models only.
agent_relevance: No clean S1/S2 split in LLMs. A frontier model's first answer is already reflective on known puzzles. Test with novel variants.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models (Studies 2, 3, 5: chain of thought and few-shot)
finding: Chain of thought acts like System 2 for GPT-3: more correct, fewer intuitive. Blocking it in ChatGPT barely hurt. A few examples teach the intuition.
numbers: davinci-003 with CoT: CRT correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29%. Semantic illusions with CoT: correct 18% to 54%. ChatGPT-3.5 told not to reason: CoT responses 97% to 0%, correct unchanged (change 4%, p=.49). ChatGPT-4 told not to reason: CoT 84% to 0%, correct 95% to 88%, intuitive 0% to 10%. Few-shot: accuracy 2% to 92% after 2 examples on one task, 12% to 92% after 7 on another, 0% to about 78% after 30 on the hardest CRT type.
limits: Small item pools; prompts differ across studies.
agent_relevance: Reasoning on or off matters a lot for weaker models and little for strong ones; skip it on easy classes (G1, direct mode).

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 reproduces the Linda conjunction fallacy but avoids cab-problem base-rate neglect; small changes in vignette wording break it. Decent human-level decisions from descriptions, fails a causal reasoning task.
numbers: Linda: chose the conjunction (fallacy). Cab: near-correct answer, unlike humans. Reported battery also includes CRT, Wason, and bandit tasks.
limits: Vignettes likely in training data; result depends on presentation order.
agent_relevance: Use perturbed variants. Right answers on canonical text are weak evidence of reasoning.

source: Kojima, Gu, Reid, Matsuo & Iwasawa (2022) Large language models are zero-shot reasoners
finding: Adding 'Let's think step by step' turns a fast zero-shot answer into a multi-step one and raises arithmetic and symbolic accuracy; framed as eliciting 'system-2 tasks'.
numbers: text-davinci-002: MultiArith 17.7% to 78.7%; GSM8K 10.4% to 40.7%. Gains on symbolic and BIG-bench logic tasks; PaLM 540B similar.
limits: Gains concentrate on multi-step problems; few-shot CoT beats zero-shot CoT.
agent_relevance: The slow-mode lever is cheap and big on multi-step problems; the open question is when to pull it.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: Took six tasks from human psychology where deliberation hurts. In three, CoT sharply lowers accuracy across models; in the others effects are mixed. Counter-evidence to 'System 2 is always better'.
numbers: o1-preview vs GPT-4o on implicit statistical learning: 36.3-point absolute drop; consistent drops across eight other LLMs. Facial recognition: CoT reduced performance in all six vision-language models.
limits: Human-model parallel is approximate (authors say so).
agent_relevance: Strong support for G1: forced reflection can hurt. Do not run slow mode on a schedule; class record decides.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models spend huge compute on trivial questions. Proposes efficiency metrics and a self-training fix that shortens reasoning without losing accuracy.
numbers: On 'what is 2 plus 3?' o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. The fix cut tokens while keeping accuracy on GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME.
limits: Open o1-like models (QwQ-32B-Preview class), not o1 itself.
agent_relevance: Adaptive depth is a real efficiency need; supports the schema's direct and no-check modes.

source: Weston & Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention (is something you might need too)
finding: S2A: the model first rewrites the input to strip irrelevant or opinionated content, then answers the cleaned input. Reduces sycophancy and distractor effects.
numbers: Factuality with distractor opinion: LLaMA-2-70B-chat 62.8% to 80.3% (oracle 82.0%). Math word problems with irrelevant sentences: 51.7% to 61.3%. Long-form objectivity up 57.4%. Single-pass variants only 71.7%.
limits: Costs an extra generation; helps only when context is contaminated; Llama-2 only.
agent_relevance: Concrete operator for S1 UNDERSTAND: extract the question and facts, drop opinion and noise, then answer.

source: Yu, Xu, Weston & Kulikov (2024) Distilling System 2 into System 1
finding: Fine-tune on outputs of slow methods (Rephrase and Respond, S2A, Branch-Solve-Merge) so a single fast pass matches them. Works for some tasks; fails for multi-step math chain of thought.
numbers: Last letter concatenation: baseline 30.0%, System 2 (2-step RaR) 39.5%, distilled 98.0%. Coin flip: 56.1% to 75.69%. Biased-input task: System 1 51.6% vs S2A 76.0% vs distilled S2A 81.3% (unbiased: 73.8, 69.3, 78.6). GSM8K: System 2 52.77% (k=1) vs distilled 7.13%; the paper says CoT distillation does not work.
limits: Needs training; our agent does not train.
agent_relevance: Task classes that compress to a fast pass are the schema's 'direct' class; long-chain maths does not compress.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: a generative agent with fast and slow thinking
finding: Agent with a small fine-tuned T5 as fast System 1 (imitation) and GPT-4 prompts as slow System 2 (planning, grounding), joined by a heuristic switch. Best on ScienceWorld.
numbers: 30 ScienceWorld task types: SwiftSage 84.7 average score vs SayCan 33.8, ReAct 36.4, Reflexion 45.3; far fewer LLM tokens per action.
limits: Switching heuristic hand-built for ScienceWorld; System 1 trained on oracle trajectories.
agent_relevance: Closest agent precedent. Switch to slow when the fast module is stuck is the impasse-detector idea in our schema.

source: Su, Sukhbaatar, Rabbat, Tian & Zheng (2025) Dualformer: controllable fast and slow thinking by randomized reasoning traces
finding: One transformer trained with randomly dropped parts of A* traces can run fast, slow or auto mode. Auto mode picks slow thinking more as mazes grow and get denser.
numbers: 30x30 maze: slow mode 97.6% optimal vs Searchformer 93.3% with 45.5% fewer steps; fast mode 80% vs 30% for solution-only; auto 96.6% with 59.9% fewer steps. Fast mode found 42 unique paths vs 3 for baseline.
limits: Synthetic planning domains; needs training.
agent_relevance: Self-chosen depth can scale with difficulty. Useful for the S0 gate design.

source: Booch et al. (2021) Thinking fast and slow in AI (AAAI)
finding: Position paper proposing AI built from Kahneman's S1 and S2 plus a metacognitive controller. Research questions, no experiments.
numbers: None; vision paper.
limits: No empirical test; takes Kahneman's theory at face value despite critiques.
agent_relevance: Shows the term is used as an architecture metaphor; this is where the 'contested' warning applies.

source: Goyal & Bengio (2022) Inductive biases for deep learning of higher-level cognition
finding: Argues deep learning lacks System-2 abilities: sequential, verbalisable, low-bandwidth through a global workspace. System 2 relies on System 1 to sample candidates, and skills migrate from explicit to implicit with practice.
numbers: None; theory. Says System 1 can run in about 100 ms, System 2 takes seconds.
limits: Conceptual; tied to Global Workspace Theory, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Supports 'System 1 samples, System 2 selects' (S3 generate, S7 select) and habit migration (S9 class record).
